analysis.one_liner: Lets one company own the newspaper and the broadcast stations in the same town.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and was never taken up by the Senate Commerce Committee, dying when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the Federal Communications Commission to erase its rule against "cross-ownership" — the ban on one company owning both a daily newspaper and a radio or TV station in the same market. The FCC would have had 90 days after the bill became law to finish the change. Eliminating the rule would let newspaper publishers buy stations in their own towns and broadcasters buy local papers, concentrating each local news market in fewer hands.
analysis.who_benefits: Large newspaper chains and broadcast station owners. A company that ran a city's daily paper could also own the AM, FM, or TV stations there, and vice versa. Because the bill set a 90-day deadline and required the FCC to eliminate the limits rather than merely reconsider them, it would have handed consolidated companies new media properties in markets they already dominated.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FCC to eliminate from its regulations any provisions limiting the granting or renewal of an AM, FM, or TV broadcast license to a party because it owns, operates, or controls a daily newspaper, including parties under common control.

Sets a 90-day deadline after enactment for the FCC to complete all action needed to make the change, so the new ownership rights would have taken effect quickly and without a fresh rulemaking process.

analysis.who_pays: Local readers and viewers. A single owner combining a town's dominant daily paper with its broadcast stations has fewer independent newsrooms checking the same institutions, less variety in local coverage, and one company deciding both what the paper reports and what the local airwaves carry. The rule the bill targeted existed to keep multiple voices in each local market.

drawbacks.text: Combining a local newspaper with local broadcast stations under one owner reduces the number of independent editorial voices covering the same community — the reason the FCC rule existed since 1975.

The strongest good-faith objection to keeping the ban was that it predates cable television and, by the late 1990s, an emerging internet, so a town's news environment was no longer limited to one paper plus local over-the-air stations; defenders of repeal argued struggling newspapers deserved access to broadcast revenue. The bill nonetheless mandated outright elimination within 90 days rather than a reconsideration weighing competition and localism.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall on the public's information environment, which is hard to price but consequential: one company controlling both a market's dominant paper and its broadcast stations removes built-in competition among local news sources. The benefits accrue to the companies that could now pair newspapers with stations. The bill gave the FCC no room to weigh localism or competition case by case — it ordered the limits wiped out on a 90-day clock — which is why it reads mainly as a favor to media companies rather than a calibrated update of media policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and expired when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain introduced S. 641 on April 24, 1997, to require the FCC to eliminate its restrictions on owning both a daily newspaper and broadcast stations in the same market.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which is the last recorded action on it.
The committee never scheduled a markup or vote, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary readers and viewers kept the existing FCC limits on combined newspaper-broadcast ownership through the end of the 105th Congress, and media companies gained nothing. The newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership rule itself remained on the books, eventually to be revisited by the FCC on its own timeline years later.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Readers and viewers; media companies gained nothing

for.name: John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-AZ); Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it was referred to the Commerce Committee he chaired, where it received no further action.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no markup, no hearing, no vote — during the two years it had jurisdiction.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other senator cosponsored, so the partisan shape of opinion on the bill never showed up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have let a company owning a market's daily paper also buy its AM, FM, and TV stations, adding broadcast revenue and broadcast reach to an already dominant print position. The public cost is fewer independent local news voices deciding what gets covered.

industries.industry: Broadcast station owners and radio/TV station groups
industries.note: Broadcasters could have acquired local daily newspapers, pairing the local airwaves with local print under common control. The 90-day mandate meant these rights would have opened up quickly, with the FCC barred from keeping any ownership limit tied to newspaper ownership.
